name: Paracetamol
description: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is a widely used over-the-counter analgesic and antipyretic agent effective for mild to moderate pain relief and fever reduction. It is one of the most commonly used medications worldwide and is available in various formulations including tablets, capsules, syrups, and intravenous preparations.
mechanism: Paracetamol inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes primarily in the central nervous system, reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Unlike NSAIDs, it has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory activity. It may also modulate the endocannabinoid system and serotonergic pathways. Its analgesic effect involves descending inhibitory pain pathways, and its antipyretic action works on the hypothalamic heat-regulating center.
indications: Mild to moderate pain including headache, dental pain, musculoskeletal pain, and postoperative pain. Fever reduction in febrile illness. First-line analgesic for patients with contraindications to NSAIDs such as peptic ulcer disease or renal impairment. Used as adjunct therapy in osteoarthritis. Intravenous paracetamol for perioperative pain management.
dosage: Adults: 500 mg to 1000 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Maximum daily dose: 4000 mg (4 g) per day for healthy adults. Reduced maximum: 2000 mg per day for patients with hepatic impairment, chronic alcohol use, or low body weight. Children: 10 to 15 mg per kg every 4 to 6 hours. Available as 500 mg tablets, 250 mg/5 mL syrup, and 1000 mg IV infusion.
side_effects: Generally well tolerated at therapeutic doses. Rare adverse effects include hepatotoxicity (especially with overdose or chronic alcohol use), skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis — very rare), thrombocytopenia, and anaphylaxis. Overdose causes severe liver necrosis potentially leading to acute liver failure and death. Symptoms of overdose include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice appearing 24 to 72 hours after ingestion.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to paracetamol. Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease. Severe alcoholism (increased risk of hepatotoxicity). Chronic malnutrition (depleted glutathione stores). Concomitant use with other hepatotoxic agents. Use with caution in renal impairment at high chronic doses.
interactions: Warfarin: paracetamol may enhance anticoagulant effect at doses above 2000 mg per day, increasing INR. Enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin, isoniazid): increase production of hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI, raising hepatotoxicity risk. Alcohol: concomitant chronic use increases risk of liver damage. Metoclopramide and domperidone: accelerate paracetamol absorption. Cholestyramine: reduces paracetamol absorption if taken within 1 hour.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; FDA Drug Label

name: Ibuprofen
description: Ibuprofen is a non-selective non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory properties. It is available over the counter in low doses (200-400 mg) and by prescription at higher doses (600-800 mg). Ibuprofen is one of the most widely used NSAIDs globally for pain and inflammation management.
mechanism: Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits both cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) enzymes, blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxanes. COX-2 inhibition reduces prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) and prostacyclin, decreasing inflammation, pain, and fever. COX-1 inhibition reduces protective gastric prostaglandins, contributing to gastrointestinal side effects. The anti-inflammatory effect also involves reduction of bradykinin and modulation of neutrophil function.
indications: Mild to moderate pain: headache, dental pain, dysmenorrhea, musculoskeletal pain, postoperative pain. Inflammatory conditions: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis. Fever reduction. Patent ductus arteriosus closure in neonates (IV formulation). Gout flare (short-term). Soft tissue injuries and sports injuries.
dosage: Adults: 200 to 400 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Maximum: 1200 mg per day for OTC use, 2400 mg per day for prescription use. Rheumatoid arthritis: 400 to 800 mg three to four times daily. Children: 5 to 10 mg per kg every 6 to 8 hours. Take with food to reduce GI irritation. Available as 200 mg, 400 mg, 600 mg tablets and 100 mg/mL oral suspension.
side_effects: Common: dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, headache, dizziness, edema. GI: gastric ulceration, GI bleeding, perforation (risk increases with age, corticosteroid use, and prolonged therapy). Cardiovascular: increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke with long-term use. Renal: fluid retention, acute kidney injury, interstitial nephritis. Hepatic: elevated liver enzymes, rare hepatotoxicity. Hematologic: prolonged bleeding time, rarely aplastic anemia. Skin: rash, rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Allergic: bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding. Severe renal or hepatic impairment. Third trimester of pregnancy (premature closure of ductus arteriosus). Severe uncontrolled heart failure. Perioperative use in coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. Aspirin-sensitive asthma or history of NSAID-induced bronchospasm. Patients with active inflammatory bowel disease.
interactions: Warfarin and anticoagulants: increased risk of bleeding. ACE inhibitors and ARBs: reduced antihypertensive effect, increased renal impairment risk. Diuretics: reduced diuretic effect, increased nephrotoxicity risk. Lithium: increased lithium levels (reduced renal clearance). Methotrexate: increased methotrexate toxicity. Aspirin: ibuprofen may reduce cardioprotective effect of low-dose aspirin (take aspirin 30 min before ibuprofen). SSRIs: increased GI bleeding risk. Corticosteroids: increased GI ulceration risk. Aminoglycosides: increased aminoglycoside levels.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; FDA Drug Label

name: Amoxicillin
description: Amoxicillin is a broad-spectrum aminopenicillin antibiotic derived from ampicillin with improved oral bioavailability. It is one of the most prescribed antibiotics worldwide and is effective against many gram-positive and some gram-negative bacteria. Amoxicillin is available as capsules, tablets, chewable tablets, and oral suspension, and is often combined with clavulanic acid (co-amoxiclav) to extend its spectrum to beta-lactamase producing organisms.
mechanism: Amoxicillin is a bactericidal beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). This binding prevents the cross-linking of peptidoglycan chains in the bacterial cell wall, leading to cell wall weakening and osmotic lysis. Amoxicillin is effective during the active multiplication phase of bacteria. It has a broader gram-negative spectrum than penicillin G due to its ability to penetrate the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria through porin channels.
indications: Upper respiratory tract infections: acute otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis (Group A streptococcal). Lower respiratory tract infections: community-acquired pneumonia, acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis. Urinary tract infections: uncomplicated UTI caused by susceptible organisms. Dental infections: dental abscess, periodontal infections. Helicobacter pylori eradication (triple therapy with PPI and clarithromycin or metronidazole). Lyme disease (early stage). Endocarditis prophylaxis in high-risk dental procedures. Neonatal sepsis.
dosage: Adults: 250 to 500 mg every 8 hours, or 500 to 875 mg every 12 hours. Severe infections: 500 mg every 8 hours or 875 mg every 12 hours. H. pylori eradication: 1000 mg twice daily for 14 days. Lyme disease: 500 mg three times daily for 14 to 21 days. Children: 25 to 50 mg per kg per day divided every 8 hours, up to 80 to 90 mg per kg per day for otitis media. Available as 250 mg and 500 mg capsules, 500 mg and 875 mg tablets, 125 mg/5 mL and 250 mg/5 mL suspensions.
side_effects: Common: diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, skin rash. GI: antibiotic-associated colitis including Clostridioides difficile infection. Allergic reactions: urticaria, maculopapular rash, anaphylaxis (rare but potentially fatal), serum sickness-like reaction. Hepatic: cholestatic jaundice (rare, typically with co-amoxiclav). Hematologic: eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia (rare). CNS: seizures at very high doses. Superinfection: oral candidiasis, vaginal candidiasis. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in Lyme disease treatment.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to amoxicillin or any penicillin antibiotic. History of severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis, angioedema) to any beta-lactam antibiotic. Infectious mononucleosis (high risk of maculopapular rash). History of amoxicillin-associated cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction. Use with caution in patients with renal impairment (dose adjustment required). Penicillin cross-reactivity with cephalosporins occurs in approximately 1 to 2% of patients.
interactions: Probenecid: reduces renal excretion of amoxicillin, increasing and prolonging blood levels. Methotrexate: amoxicillin reduces renal clearance of methotrexate, increasing toxicity risk. Warfarin: enhanced anticoagulant effect, monitor INR. Oral contraceptives: theoretical reduced efficacy (clinical significance debated). Allopurinol: increased incidence of skin rash. Aminoglycosides: synergistic bactericidal effect but do not mix in same IV line. Tetracyclines and chloramphenicol: may antagonize bactericidal effect of amoxicillin.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; FDA Drug Label

name: Metformin
description: Metformin is the first-line oral antihyperglycemic agent for type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is a biguanide that lowers blood glucose through multiple mechanisms without causing hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy. Metformin has been used for over 60 years and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List. It may also have benefits for weight management, cardiovascular protection, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
mechanism: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production primarily by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis through activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). It also decreases intestinal absorption of glucose, improves insulin sensitivity by enhancing peripheral glucose uptake and utilization in skeletal muscle, and may modulate gut microbiome composition. Metformin does not stimulate insulin secretion and therefore does not cause hypoglycemia. It reduces the respiratory chain complex I in mitochondria, increasing the AMP to ATP ratio, which activates AMPK.
indications: Type 2 diabetes mellitus: first-line pharmacotherapy, especially in overweight and obese patients. Can be used as monotherapy or in combination with other antidiabetic agents (sulfonylureas, SGLT2 inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, insulin). Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): off-label use for insulin resistance and ovulation induction. Prediabetes: may delay progression to type 2 diabetes. Gestational diabetes: second-line after insulin in some guidelines. Weight management: may promote modest weight loss.
dosage: Initial dose: 500 mg once or twice daily with meals, or 850 mg once daily. Titrate by 500 mg per week as tolerated. Maintenance: 1500 to 2000 mg per day in divided doses. Maximum: 2550 mg per day (immediate release), 2000 mg per day (extended release). Extended-release formulation taken once daily with evening meal. Available as 500 mg, 850 mg, and 1000 mg tablets and 500 mg/5 mL oral solution. Renal impairment: eGFR 30 to 45: reduce dose, eGFR below 30: contraindicated.
side_effects: Common: diarrhea (especially during titration), nausea, vomiting, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, metallic taste. GI side effects often improve over time or with extended-release formulation. Serious but rare: lactic acidosis (mortality approximately 50%, risk increased with renal impairment, hepatic disease, heart failure, sepsis, and alcohol abuse). Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use (monitor annually). Very rare: cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions including erythema multiforme.
contraindications: Severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2). Acute or chronic metabolic acidosis including diabetic ketoacidosis. Acute conditions with risk of tissue hypoxia (sepsis, shock, acute heart failure, acute MI). Severe hepatic impairment. Heavy alcohol use. Administration of iodinated contrast within 48 hours (temporary discontinuation). History of lactic acidosis. Hypersensitivity to metformin.
interactions: Alcohol: enhances the effect on lactate metabolism, increasing lactic acidosis risk. Iodinated contrast media: risk of acute renal failure and lactic acidosis — discontinue metformin at time of or before procedure. Cationic drugs eliminated by renal tubular secretion (ranitidine, trimethoprim, cimetidine): may increase metformin levels by competing for renal transport. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (topiramate, acetazolamide): increase lactic acidosis risk. Insulin and sulfonylureas: risk of hypoglycemia when combined. Corticosteroids: may reduce metformin efficacy.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; ADA Standards of Care 2024; FDA Drug Label

name: Warfarin
description: Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant and vitamin K antagonist used for the prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disorders. It has a narrow therapeutic index requiring regular INR monitoring. Warfarin is one of the most commonly prescribed anticoagulants globally despite the availability of newer direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). Its long half-life and extensive drug interaction profile require careful management.
mechanism: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase complex 1 (VKORC1), preventing the recycling of vitamin K from its epoxide form to the reduced form. Reduced vitamin K is a cofactor for the gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X in the liver. Without carboxylation, these factors cannot bind calcium and participate in the coagulation cascade. Warfarin also inhibits anticoagulant proteins C and S. The initial procoagulant effect of protein C suppression creates a transient hypercoagulable state at therapy initiation.
indications: Atrial fibrillation: stroke prevention in non-valvular and valvular atrial fibrillation. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT): treatment and prevention of recurrence. Pulmonary embolism (PE): treatment and secondary prevention. Mechanical heart valves: anticoagulation of choice (DOACs contraindicated). Antiphospholipid syndrome: preferred over DOACs. Post-myocardial infarction: in high-risk patients with mural thrombus. Peripheral arterial embolism prevention.
dosage: Individualized based on INR response. Initial dose: 2.5 to 5 mg daily for most adults (lower initial dose for elderly, hepatic impairment, heart failure, concurrent medications). Higher initial dose (7.5 to 10 mg) may be used in young healthy patients. Maintenance: typically 2 to 10 mg daily, adjusted to target INR. Target INR: 2.0 to 3.0 for most indications, 2.5 to 3.5 for mechanical mitral valves. INR monitoring: daily during initiation, then weekly, then monthly when stable. Available as 1 mg, 2 mg, 2.5 mg, 3 mg, 4 mg, 5 mg, 6 mg, 7.5 mg, and 10 mg color-coded tablets.
side_effects: Major: hemorrhage (most serious — intracranial, GI, retroperitoneal), occurring in 1 to 3% of patients per year. Minor: bruising, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, hematuria. Skin: warfarin-induced skin necrosis (typically days 3 to 8, due to protein C depletion, higher risk in patients with protein C or S deficiency), calciphylaxis (rare). Purple toe syndrome (cholesterol microembolization). Hair loss (rare). Osteoporosis with long-term use. Teratogenicity: embryopathy in first trimester, CNS abnormalities in any trimester.
contraindications: Active major bleeding. Hemorrhagic stroke. Recent or planned surgery with high bleeding risk. Severe uncontrolled hypertension. Bacterial endocarditis (risk of mycotic aneurysm rupture). Pericarditis and pericardial effusion. Pregnancy (teratogenic — use heparin instead). Severe thrombocytopenia. Recent GI hemorrhage. Non-compliant patients or inability to monitor INR. Hypersensitivity to warfarin.
interactions: Warfarin has an extensive interaction profile with over 200 clinically significant interactions. CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitors increase warfarin effect: amiodarone (reduce dose by 30 to 50%), fluconazole, metronidazole, fluoxetine, omeprazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. CYP inducers decrease warfarin effect: rifampicin (may need 2 to 5x dose increase), carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's Wort, chronic alcohol use. Vitamin K intake variations affect INR stability. NSAIDs and aspirin increase bleeding risk. Broad-spectrum antibiotics alter gut flora and vitamin K production. Acetaminophen above 2 g/day potentiates anticoagulant effect.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; ACC/AHA Guidelines; FDA Drug Label

name: Aspirin
description: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug with unique irreversible antiplatelet properties. At low doses it is used for cardiovascular protection, at intermediate doses for pain and fever, and at high doses for inflammatory conditions. Aspirin is one of the oldest and most studied medications in pharmacological history, with applications spanning cardiology, rheumatology, oncology, and primary care.
mechanism: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates serine residues on cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and COX-2 enzymes. At low doses (75 to 100 mg), aspirin permanently inhibits platelet COX-1, preventing thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis for the entire 7 to 10 day lifespan of the platelet, providing sustained antiplatelet effect. At higher doses, it also inhibits COX-2, providing analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects. The irreversible nature of platelet inhibition distinguishes aspirin from other NSAIDs which reversibly inhibit COX. Aspirin also triggers lipoxin synthesis via acetylated COX-2, contributing to anti-inflammatory resolution.
indications: Cardiovascular: low-dose (75 to 100 mg daily) for secondary prevention of myocardial infarction, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease. Acute coronary syndrome: 300 mg loading dose. Primary prevention in high-risk patients (controversial, risk-benefit individualized). Analgesic and antipyretic: headache, dental pain, musculoskeletal pain, fever. Inflammatory: rheumatoid arthritis, rheumatic fever, Kawasaki disease (high doses). Colorectal cancer prevention (off-label, emerging evidence). Preeclampsia prevention in high-risk pregnant women (low-dose, 75 to 150 mg).
dosage: Antiplatelet: 75 to 100 mg once daily. Acute MI loading: 300 mg chewed immediately. Analgesic/antipyretic: 300 to 600 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 4 g per day. Anti-inflammatory: 4 to 6 g per day in divided doses (rarely used). Kawasaki disease: high dose (80 to 100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses) for initial phase, then low dose (3 to 5 mg/kg/day) for 6 to 8 weeks. Available as 75 mg, 100 mg, 300 mg, and 500 mg tablets, enteric-coated formulations, and dispersible tablets.
side_effects: Common: dyspepsia, heartburn, nausea, abdominal pain. GI: gastric erosions, peptic ulceration, GI bleeding (dose-dependent, reduced with enteric coating). Hemorrhagic: increased bleeding time, hemorrhagic stroke (small absolute risk at low doses). Hypersensitivity: aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD) — nasal polyps, asthma, and bronchospasm. Skin: urticaria, angioedema. Reye syndrome: aspirin in children with viral illness (fever, encephalopathy, hepatic failure). Tinnitus and hearing loss at high doses (salicylism). Renal: impaired renal function at chronic high doses.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs. Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter triad). Active peptic ulceration or GI bleeding. Severe hepatic impairment. Children under 16 years (Reye syndrome risk). Severe renal impairment. Hemorrhagic disorders including hemophilia. Third trimester of pregnancy. Concomitant use with methotrexate at high doses. Gout (low-dose aspirin increases uric acid levels).
interactions: Warfarin and anticoagulants: significantly increased bleeding risk. Other NSAIDs: combined use increases GI bleeding risk; ibuprofen may reduce cardioprotective effect of aspirin. Clopidogrel: dual antiplatelet therapy increases bleeding risk but is standard post-ACS and post-stent. Methotrexate: reduced renal clearance, increased toxicity. ACE inhibitors: reduced antihypertensive effect. Corticosteroids: increased GI ulceration risk. SSRIs: increased GI bleeding risk. Alcohol: increased GI bleeding risk. Probenecid: reduces uricosuric effect of high-dose aspirin. Valproic acid: displaced from protein binding, increased free levels.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; FDA Drug Label; ESC Guidelines

name: Omeprazole
description: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly blocks the hydrogen-potassium ATPase (proton pump) on gastric parietal cells, reducing gastric acid secretion. It is one of the most prescribed medications worldwide for acid-related gastrointestinal disorders. Omeprazole is available over the counter and by prescription in various formulations.
mechanism: Omeprazole is a prodrug that is absorbed in the small intestine and reaches parietal cells via the bloodstream. In the acidic environment of the parietal cell canaliculus, omeprazole is converted to its active sulfenamide form, which forms a covalent disulfide bond with cysteine residues on the H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump). This irreversible inhibition blocks the final step of gastric acid secretion, reducing both basal and stimulated acid production. Onset of action is 1 to 3 hours, but maximal acid suppression occurs after 3 to 5 days of repeated dosing as more proton pumps are inactivated.
indications: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD): first-line treatment for erosive esophagitis and symptom relief. Peptic ulcer disease: duodenal ulcers, gastric ulcers, and NSAID-induced ulcers. Helicobacter pylori eradication: as part of triple or quadruple therapy. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: high-dose therapy for acid hypersecretion. Stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients. Barrett esophagus: acid suppression to prevent progression. Dyspepsia: empiric therapy. Prevention of aspiration pneumonitis preoperatively.
dosage: GERD: 20 mg once daily for 4 to 8 weeks, maintenance 10 to 20 mg daily. Duodenal ulcer: 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks. Gastric ulcer: 20 to 40 mg once daily for 4 to 8 weeks. H. pylori eradication: 20 mg twice daily for 14 days. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: 60 mg once daily, adjusted up to 120 mg three times daily. Children: 0.7 to 3.3 mg/kg per day. Take 30 to 60 minutes before meals. Available as 10 mg, 20 mg, and 40 mg capsules and 2 mg/mL oral suspension.
side_effects: Common: headache, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, flatulence, constipation. Long-term risks: hypomagnesemia (can cause arrhythmias and seizures), vitamin B12 deficiency, increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, osteoporosis-related fractures (hip, spine, wrist), chronic kidney disease. Fundic gland polyps (benign, dose and duration dependent). Acute interstitial nephritis (rare). Possible increased risk of dementia (controversial, conflicting evidence). Hypocalcemia and hypokalemia secondary to hypomagnesemia.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to omeprazole or other proton pump inhibitors. Concomitant use with rilpivirine (reduced rilpivirine levels, risk of HIV treatment failure). Use with caution in severe hepatic impairment (dose adjustment). Long-term use should be at the lowest effective dose and for the shortest duration. Not recommended in children under 1 year.
interactions: Clopidogrel: omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, reducing conversion of clopidogrel to active metabolite (use pantoprazole instead). Methotrexate: PPIs may reduce renal clearance. Diazepam and phenytoin: omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, increasing levels. Tacrolimus: increased tacrolimus levels. Iron and calcium supplements: reduced absorption due to decreased gastric acidity. Ketoconazole and itraconazole: reduced absorption. Rilpivirine: significantly reduced levels. Digoxin: slightly increased absorption. Voriconazole: mutual effect on levels.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; FDA Drug Label

name: Atorvastatin
description: Atorvastatin is a synthetic HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor and the most prescribed statin worldwide. It is a potent lipid-lowering agent used for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Atorvastatin has a long half-life allowing flexible dosing and is available in generic form. Brand name Lipitor was the best-selling pharmaceutical drug in history.
mechanism: Atorvastatin competitively inhibits 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis. By blocking mevalonate production, intracellular cholesterol decreases, upregulating hepatic LDL receptor expression on cell surfaces. This increases clearance of LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Atorvastatin also reduces VLDL production, increases HDL cholesterol modestly, and has pleiotropic effects including anti-inflammatory activity, endothelial function improvement, and plaque stabilization. Active metabolites contribute to the extended duration of action.
indications: Primary hypercholesterolemia and mixed dyslipidemia: LDL-C reduction. Familial hypercholesterolemia. Secondary prevention of cardiovascular events: post-MI, post-stroke, peripheral arterial disease. Primary prevention: in patients with elevated cardiovascular risk (diabetes, 10-year ASCVD risk above 7.5%). Diabetic dyslipidemia. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk reduction. Heterozygous and homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
dosage: Initial: 10 to 20 mg once daily. Moderate intensity: 10 to 20 mg daily (30 to 49% LDL reduction). High intensity: 40 to 80 mg daily (50% or greater LDL reduction). Maximum: 80 mg daily. Take at any time of day (longer half-life than other statins). Renal impairment: no dose adjustment. Hepatic impairment: contraindicated. Elderly: no specific adjustment. Available as 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, and 80 mg tablets.
side_effects: Common: myalgia (muscle pain, 5 to 10%), headache, nasopharyngitis, arthralgia, diarrhea, nausea. Muscular: myopathy (CK elevation with symptoms), rhabdomyolysis (very rare but serious, risk increases with dose, age, hypothyroidism, and interacting drugs). Hepatic: elevated transaminases (3x ULN in 0.5 to 2%), hepatotoxicity (rare). Metabolic: new-onset diabetes mellitus (9 to 12% increased risk). Cognitive: memory complaints (rare, reversible). Peripheral neuropathy (rare). Tendon disorders (rare).
contraindications: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevation of hepatic transaminases. Pregnancy and lactation (cholesterol essential for fetal development). Hypersensitivity to atorvastatin or any component. Concomitant use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, HIV protease inhibitors, clarithromycin) at 40 to 80 mg doses. Cyclosporine: do not exceed 10 mg atorvastatin.
interactions: CYP3A4 inhibitors increase atorvastatin levels: clarithromycin, erythromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, diltiazem, verapamil, grapefruit juice (large quantities). Cyclosporine: significantly increased atorvastatin exposure, limit to 10 mg. Fibrates (gemfibrozil especially): increased myopathy risk (fenofibrate preferred). Niacin at high doses: increased myopathy risk. Warfarin: enhanced anticoagulant effect, monitor INR. Digoxin: slightly increased digoxin levels. Rifampicin: reduced atorvastatin levels (CYP3A4 induction). Colchicine: increased myopathy risk. Oral contraceptives: increased norethindrone and ethinyl estradiol levels.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; ACC/AHA Lipid Guidelines; FDA Drug Label

name: Lisinopril
description: Lisinopril is a long-acting angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor used for hypertension, heart failure, and diabetic nephropathy. It is a lysine analog of enalaprilat and does not require hepatic activation (unlike enalapril). Lisinopril is one of the most prescribed antihypertensives in the world and is available in generic form.
mechanism: Lisinopril inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), a peptidyl dipeptidase that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and degrades bradykinin. By blocking angiotensin II production, lisinopril reduces vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion (reducing sodium and water retention), and sympathetic nervous system activation. Accumulation of bradykinin contributes to vasodilation and the characteristic dry cough side effect. The net effect is reduced peripheral vascular resistance, reduced blood pressure, reduced cardiac preload and afterload, and cardioprotective and renoprotective effects.
indications: Hypertension: first-line antihypertensive, can be used as monotherapy or in combination. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): improves survival, reduces hospitalizations. Post-myocardial infarction: within 24 hours of anterior MI to prevent ventricular remodeling. Diabetic nephropathy: renoprotective, reduces proteinuria and slows progression of chronic kidney disease. Acute myocardial infarction: within 24 hours in hemodynamically stable patients.
dosage: Hypertension: initial 10 mg once daily, maintenance 20 to 40 mg daily, maximum 80 mg daily. Heart failure: initial 2.5 to 5 mg once daily, titrate to target 20 to 40 mg daily as tolerated. Post-MI: initial 5 mg within 24 hours, then 5 mg after 24 hours, 10 mg after 48 hours, then 10 mg daily. Diabetic nephropathy: 10 to 20 mg daily. Renal impairment: eGFR 10 to 30: initial 2.5 to 5 mg daily, eGFR below 10: initial 2.5 mg daily. Available as 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg, and 40 mg tablets.
side_effects: Common: dry persistent cough (5 to 20%, class effect), dizziness, headache, fatigue, hypotension (especially first dose), hyperkalemia. Serious: angioedema (0.1 to 0.7%, higher in Black patients, can be life-threatening if laryngeal), acute kidney injury (especially in renal artery stenosis), hyperkalemia (risk increased with potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, renal impairment), fetal toxicity (teratogenic in second and third trimesters). Rare: hepatotoxicity (cholestatic jaundice), neutropenia (in renal impairment or collagen vascular disease), pancreatitis, taste disturbance.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to lisinopril or any ACE inhibitor. History of angioedema (hereditary, idiopathic, or ACE inhibitor-related). Bilateral renal artery stenosis or unilateral in solitary kidney. Pregnancy and lactation. Concomitant use with aliskiren in diabetic patients. Concomitant use with neprilysin inhibitors (sacubitril) within 36 hours. Hereditary or idiopathic angioedema. Severe renal impairment without monitoring.
interactions: Potassium supplements and potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride, triamterene): hyperkalemia risk. Diuretics: enhanced hypotensive effect, risk of first-dose hypotension. NSAIDs: reduced antihypertensive effect, increased renal impairment risk, hyperkalemia. Lithium: increased lithium levels (reduced renal clearance). Aliskiren: increased hyperkalemia and renal impairment risk. Sacubitril (ARNI): must not be given within 36 hours (angioedema risk). Dual RAAS blockade (ARB + ACE inhibitor): increased adverse effects without benefit. Mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus): increased angioedema risk.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; AHA/ACC Heart Failure Guidelines; FDA Drug Label

name: Sertraline
description: Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) widely used as first-line pharmacotherapy for major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, and several other psychiatric conditions. It has a favorable side effect profile compared to older antidepressants and is one of the most prescribed psychiatric medications globally. Sertraline is available as a generic medication.
mechanism: Sertraline selectively inhibits the serotonin transporter (SERT) at the presynaptic neuron, blocking the reuptake of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) from the synaptic cleft. This increases serotonin availability in the synapse, enhancing serotonergic neurotransmission. Downstream adaptive changes include desensitization of presynaptic 5-HT1A autoreceptors, upregulation of postsynaptic receptors, and modulation of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). These adaptive changes explain the 2 to 4 week delay in therapeutic onset. Sertraline has minimal affinity for muscarinic, histaminergic, and alpha-adrenergic receptors.
indications: Major depressive disorder (MDD): first-line treatment. Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Panic disorder with or without agoraphobia. Social anxiety disorder (social phobia). Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Off-label: premature ejaculation, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, vasomotor symptoms of menopause.
dosage: MDD and OCD: initial 50 mg once daily, increase by 25 to 50 mg at weekly intervals, maximum 200 mg daily. Panic disorder: start at 25 mg daily for one week, then increase to 50 mg daily. PTSD: 50 to 200 mg daily. PMDD: 50 mg daily (continuous or luteal phase dosing). Take in the morning or evening, with or without food. Pediatric OCD: 6 to 12 years start at 25 mg, 13 to 17 years start at 50 mg. Available as 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg tablets and 20 mg/mL oral concentrate.
side_effects: Common: nausea (most common, usually transient), diarrhea, insomnia, dizziness, headache, dry mouth, drowsiness, sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, delayed ejaculation, anorgasmia), tremor, increased sweating, appetite changes. GI: weight gain or loss. Sexual dysfunction: affects up to 30 to 40% of patients, may persist after discontinuation (PSSD — post-SSRI sexual dysfunction, rare). Serious: serotonin syndrome (especially with concurrent serotonergic drugs), suicidal ideation (increased risk in children and young adults under 25), hyponatremia (SIADH, especially in elderly), increased bleeding risk (platelet serotonin depletion), QT prolongation (dose-dependent, rare at therapeutic doses). Discontinuation syndrome: dizziness, nausea, headache, irritability, insomnia, electric shock sensations (brain zaps).
contraindications: Concomitant use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs): must have 14-day washout. Concomitant use with pimozide. Hypersensitivity to sertraline. Concomitant use with disulfiram (oral concentrate contains alcohol). Use caution in bipolar disorder (risk of mania), seizure disorders, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, and in patients with bleeding risk.
interactions: MAOIs: serotonin syndrome (potentially fatal) — absolutely contraindicated. Other serotonergic drugs (tramadol, triptans, lithium, St. John's Wort, fentanyl): serotonin syndrome risk. Pimozide: QT prolongation. Warfarin: increased bleeding risk (monitor INR). NSAIDs and aspirin: increased GI bleeding risk. CYP2D6 substrates (codeine, tamoxifen): sertraline is a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor, may reduce conversion to active metabolites. Phenytoin: sertraline may increase phenytoin levels. Lithium: enhanced serotonergic effect, monitor for toxicity. Alcohol: additive CNS depression. Digoxin: may reduce digoxin levels. Cimetidine: significantly increases sertraline levels.
source: FDA Drug Label; APA Practice Guidelines; NICE Guidelines; BNF 2024

name: Salbutamol
description: Salbutamol (albuterol in the US) is a short-acting selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist used as a rescue medication for acute bronchospasm. It is the most prescribed bronchodilator worldwide and is available as metered-dose inhaler (MDI), dry powder inhaler (DPI), nebulizer solution, oral tablets, and intravenous injection. Salbutamol is a cornerstone of asthma and COPD management.
mechanism: Salbutamol selectively stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle cells. Receptor activation activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), which activates protein kinase A (PKA). PKA phosphorylates and inactivates myosin light chain kinase, leading to smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation. Salbutamol also inhibits mast cell mediator release, enhances mucociliary clearance, and may reduce microvascular permeability. At high doses, beta-1 selectivity decreases, potentially causing cardiac effects.
indications: Acute asthma: first-line rescue medication for acute bronchospasm. Asthma management: as-needed short-acting beta agonist (SABA) for symptom relief. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: prophylactic use 15 to 30 minutes before exercise. COPD: rescue bronchodilation. Acute bronchitis: bronchodilation in wheezy patients. Hyperkalemia: acute management (shifts potassium intracellularly). Premature labor: tocolytic (off-label, largely replaced by safer agents). Status asthmaticus: nebulized or IV in acute severe asthma.
dosage: MDI (100 mcg/puff): 1 to 2 puffs as needed for symptoms, maximum 8 puffs per day. Nebulizer: 2.5 to 5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses in acute severe asthma, then every 1 to 4 hours as needed. Oral: 2 to 4 mg three to four times daily (rarely used). IV: 3 to 20 mcg/min by infusion (hospital use). Children: 1 to 2 puffs MDI or 2.5 mg nebulizer. Spacer device recommended with MDI for children and poorly coordinated patients.
side_effects: Common: tremor (especially hands), tachycardia, palpitations, headache, nervousness, dizziness, throat irritation. Muscular: muscle cramps (due to intracellular potassium shift). Metabolic: hypokalemia (dose-dependent, clinically significant in patients on diuretics or digoxin), hyperglycemia, lactic acidosis (rare, with frequent nebulization). Cardiovascular: arrhythmias (rare at therapeutic doses), chest pain. Paradoxical bronchospasm (rare but serious). Tolerance: may develop with regular use (loss of bronchoprotective effect), highlighting need for ICS as controller therapy.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to salbutamol or any component. Tachyarrhythmias. Use with caution in cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism, seizure disorders, and pheochromocytoma. Not recommended as sole therapy for persistent asthma (must use with inhaled corticosteroid). Hypokalemia: use cautiously.
interactions: Beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol): antagonize bronchodilator effect, may cause severe bronchospasm in asthmatic patients. Diuretics (loop and thiazide): additive hypokalemia. Digoxin: hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk. MAOIs and tricyclic antidepressants: potentiate cardiovascular effects of salbutamol. Corticosteroids: additive hypokalemia. Xanthines (theophylline): additive bronchodilation and hypokalemia. Sympathomimetic amines: additive effects. Potassium-depleting medications: increased hypokalemia risk.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; GINA Guidelines 2024; BNF 2024; FDA Drug Label

name: Ciprofloxacin
description: Ciprofloxacin is a second-generation fluoroquinolone antibiotic with broad-spectrum activity against gram-negative bacteria and moderate activity against some gram-positive organisms. It has excellent oral bioavailability and tissue penetration, making it effective for a wide range of infections. Ciprofloxacin is available as tablets, oral suspension, IV infusion, and otic/ophthalmic preparations.
mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for DNA replication, transcription, and recombination. DNA gyrase introduces negative supercoils in bacterial DNA, while topoisomeraserelaxes supercoiled DNA during replication. By inhibiting these enzymes, ciprofloxacin prevents bacterial DNA replication and causes double-strand DNA breaks leading to bacterial cell death. The bactericidal activity is concentration-dependent. Ciprofloxacin has a post-antibiotic effect lasting 1 to 6 hours.
indications: Urinary tract infections (including complicated UTI and pyelonephritis): first-line empiric therapy in areas with low resistance. Acute bacterial sinusitis: second-line when other agents fail. Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis. Infectious diarrhea: traveler's diarrhea caused by E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella. Anthrax inhalation exposure: post-exposure prophylaxis and treatment. Pseudomuginosa infections: particularly in cystic fibrosis. Bone and joint infections: osteomyelitis. Complicated intra-abdominal infections: in combination with metronidazole. Gonorrhea: only in areas with confirmed susceptibility. Prostatitis. Febrile neutropenia.
dosage: UTI: 250 to 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 to 14 days depending on severity. Complicated UTI/pyelonephritis: 500 mg every 12 hours for 7 to 14 days. Respiratory infections: 500 to 750 mg every 12 hours for 7 to 14 days. Infectious diarrhea: 500 mg every 12 hours for 3 to 7 days. Anthrax: 500 mg every 12 hours for 60 days. IV: 200 to 400 mg every 8 to 12 hours by infusion over 60 minutes. Renal impairment: CrCl 30 to 50: reduce by 50% if dose above 500 mg. Available as 100 mg, 250 mg, 500 mg, and 750 mg tablets.
side_effects: Common: nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, rash. CNS: insomnia, restlessness, seizures (lower seizure threshold), peripheral neuropathy (may be irreversible), tendon pain. Musculoskeletal: tendinitis and tendon rupture (especially Achilles tendon, risk increased with age over 60, corticosteroids, organ transplant), arthralgia, myalgia. Cardiovascular: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes (rare). Hepatic: elevated transaminases, hepatotoxicity (rare). Renal: crystalluria (adequate hydration important), acute kidney injury. Skin: photosensitivity, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (rare). GI: Clostridioides difficile infection. Aortic aneurysm and dissection (rare, risk increased in elderly with existing aortic disease). Retinal detachment (controversial, possible small risk). Dysglycemia in diabetic patients.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ciprofloxacin or other fluoroquinolones. Tendon disorders related to fluoroquinolone use. Myasthenia gravis (may exacerbate muscle weakness). Concomitant use with tizanidine (dramatically increased tizanidine levels). Children and adolescents (except for specific indications like anthrax, complicated UTI) due to cartilage damage risk. QT prolongation: avoid in patients with congenital long QT syndrome, uncorrected electrolyte imbalance, or concurrent QT-prolonging drugs.
interactions: Ciprofloxacin is a potent CYP1A2 inhibitor. Theophylline and caffeine: increased levels (seizure risk). Tizanidine: contraindicated (5 to 8-fold increased tizanidine levels). Warfarin: enhanced anticoagulant effect. Antacids, iron, calcium, zinc, sucralfate: significantly reduced ciprofloxacin absorption (take 2 hours before or 6 hours after). Probenecid: reduced renal clearance of ciprofloxacin. Cyclosporine: increased nephrotoxicity risk. Phenytoin: variable effects on levels. Duloxetine: increased duloxetine levels. Methotrexate: reduced renal clearance. NSAIDs: increased seizure risk. Oral hypoglycemics (glibenclamide): hypoglycemia risk. QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics): additive QT prolongation.
source: WHO Essential Medicines List; BNF 2024; FDA Black Box Warning; IDSA Guidelines
